title_r: Tracking Affect Ratings Over Time (TAROT) task: Replication and Extension Study
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This registration outlines the literature background, study procedures and measures, hypotheses, and plan for analysis.

summary: Pre-registration: 
Tracking Affect Ratings Over Time (TAROT) task: Replication and Extension Study
 
     Anxiety disorders are highly prevalent, impacting 33% of adults in the United States in their lifetime (Kessler, Petukhova, Sampson, Zaslavsky, & Wittchen, 2012). Individuals who experience frequent and intense anxiety often report impaired functioning in school, work, relationships, and physical health (Kroenke, Spitzer, Williams, Monahan, & Löwe, 2007). One set of factors implicated in the onset and maintenance of anxiety symptoms is anxiety-linked cognitive biases. Specifically, there is evidence that highly anxious individuals process emotional stimuli in distinct ways compared to their less anxious peers. For instance, more (vs. less) anxious individuals tend to more quickly orient their attention to threatening (vs. neutral) stimuli (Armstrong & Olatunji, 2012; Bar-Haim, Lamy, Pergamin, Bakermans-Kranenburg, & Van Ijzendoorn, 2007), and have more difficulty disengaging from emotional stimuli, including threatening words and faces (Armstrong & Olatunji, 2012; Fox, Russo, & Dutton, 2002; Salemink, van den Hout, & Kindt, 2007). Highly anxious individuals (vs. those lower in anxiety) also tend to interpret emotionally ambiguous information (e.g., sentences) in negative ways (Amir, Prouvost, & Kuckertz, 2012; Eysenck, Mogg, May, Richards, & Mathews, 1991; Mathews, 2012), and expect negative future outcomes (Alden, Taylor, Mellings, & Laposa, 2008; MacLeod, Tata, Kentish, & Jacobsen, 1997; Morina, Deeprose, Pusowski, Schmid, & Holmes, 2011). Lastly, there is evidence that highly anxious individuals interpret positive information in negative ways (Alden et al., 2008), and have difficulty reaping the benefits of positive events (Farmer & Kashdan, 2012). 
     Although there is ample evidence that higher anxiety vulnerability is linked with biased processing of emotional information, we know relatively little about the emotional context (in terms of the impact of pre-existing emotional cues) in which these biases unfold. For instance, there is limited knowledge of the process through which biased responding unfolds, as well as of the ways in which previously encountered emotional information influences how individuals process subsequent emotional stimuli. This is due, in part, to the way cognitive biases are commonly assessed: frequently used tasks (e.g., the emotional Stroop, the emotional spatial cuing paradigm) assess participants’ cognitive biases by presenting them with threatening and neutral stimuli and comparing the speed of their responses to these different kinds of material (Bar-Haim et al., 2007). Participants’ responses are then used to arrive at a single score that captures a given anxiety-linked cognitive bias (e.g., difficulty disengaging from emotional stimuli). As such, these tasks give us a static snapshot of participants’ biased responding, but do not capture the many stages of the process as it unfolds over time. Moreover, these tasks often do not take into account the potential influence of previously encountered information – such as exposure to prior threatening material— on how individuals process novel information. These factors mean we are missing critical information about when and how a process is biased for anxious individuals given individuals continuously process emotional information in their daily lives, and do not begin processing each emotional experience from a “neutral” starting point. We can thus improve our assessment of anxiety-linked biases by incorporating the emotional context during which they unfold. 
     The Tracking Affect Ratings over Time (TAROT) task, developed by Fua and Teachman (2017), holds promise as a measure of cognitive biases and their emotional context. In this task, participants listen to scenarios composed of neutral, positive, and negative events tied to social or physical health stressors (e.g., going to the doctor’s office). As each scenario unfolds, participants continuously report their affect as it changes in real time using a slider scale (-1,000 = Very Negative; 1,000 = Very Positive). Several features of this task allow for the assessment of anxiety linked-biases as well as their emotional context. First, by presenting individuals with differently valenced events within each scenario, the TAROT task allows the examination of how prior emotional information influences processing of subsequent emotional information (e.g., do more highly anxious individuals get “stuck” on negative information and respond more negatively to subsequent positive events?). Second, valenced events are presented in different orders across scenarios, allowing analysis of how individuals’ affective responses vary as a function of the order in which emotional stimuli unfold (e.g., negative events before positive and neutral, positive before neutral and negative, and so on). Third, by assessing individuals’ affective responses to multiple events of different valences, the TAROT task efficiently measures multiple cognitive biases at the same time. Taken together, these features of the TAROT task make it a useful tool to advance our understanding of how individuals dynamically process anxiety-relevant emotional material. 
Evidence of the TAROT’s utility has been reported in one study to date. Fua and Teachman (2017) recruited 141 undergraduate participants with varying levels of social anxiety symptoms and anxiety sensitivity levels. Participants listened to 36 narratives (18 social and 18 physical) containing neutral, positive, and negative events and continuously reported their affect as each narrative unfolded. Participants’ continuous affective responses to the valenced events were used to index several forms of biased responding to emotional information (e.g., rating neutral stimuli as more negative). TAROT indices displayed strong internal consistency reliability, construct validity, and incremental validity. Additionally, they related in the expected ways with measures of trait anxiety. For instance, participants higher (vs. lower) in physical anxiety sensitivity (as measured by the physical subscale of the Anxiety Sensitivity Index; Peterson & Reiss, 1992) had more negative interpretations of all valenced events, quicker affective responses to negative events, and more negative ratings of positive events. TAROT indices also displayed several of the hypothesized associations with social anxiety symptoms. Additionally, results suggested that prior emotional information influences the processing of subsequent material, such that more (vs. less) anxiety sensitive individuals reported more negative affective ratings of positive and neutral events when they were presented after negative ones within a given scenario. Taken together, results from this initial study suggest that the TAROT is an efficient and psychometrically sound tool to assess individuals’ anxiety-linked biases within an ever-changing emotional context. 
     The TAROT task is also a potentially useful tool to learn more about how anxiety-linked biases predict individuals’ responses to stressors, but initial results did not show the expected associations. Fua and Teachman (2017) tested the predictive validity of TAROT indices with respect to self-reported subjective distress tied to social and physical stressor tasks (the social stressor involved giving an impromptu speech, and the physical stressor was the candle-blowing task, which entails pretending to vigorously blow out a flame approximately 100 times per minute, and typically induces temporary dizziness and lightheadedness). Contrary to hypotheses, TAROT indices did not robustly predict individuals’ subjective distress during either task. This is surprising given prior evidence that anxiety-linked cognitive biases predict individuals’ responses during physical stressors, with small-to-medium effect sizes (Cabeleira et al., 2014; Gordon & Teachman, 2008). As such, it remains important to evaluate whether anxiety-linked biases, as measured by the TAROT task, are useful predictors of emotional vulnerability to a stressor. 

I. Present Study
     The present study aims to replicate Fua and Teachman’s (2017) findings regarding the psychometric properties of the TAROT task and the associations between TAROT indices and physical anxiety sensitivity levels. In addition, the current study extends this prior work in several ways. First, whereas Fua and Teachman recruited undergraduates with varying levels of anxiety sensitivity (and social anxiety), the present study used an extreme groups design, such that individuals were recruited if they scored high or low on the physical concerns subscale of the Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3 (ASI-3; Taylor et al., 2007) 1. This sampling approach was selected because individuals higher (vs. lower) in anxiety sensitivity are more likely to express anxiety-linked biases (Cabeleira et al., 2014; Clerkin, Beard, Fisher, & Schofield, 2015). As such, this approach provides the opportunity to further characterize the cognitive biases assessed by the TAROT among a clinical analogue sample and more directly compare biases among high vs. low-anxiety sensitive individuals.
     A second way the current study extends Fua and Teachman is by testing the associations between TAROT indices and responses to a more elaborate physical stressor that allows for delineation of anticipatory anxiety, acute stress, and recovery phases using multiple modes of assessment. Fua and Teachman measured individuals’ subjective distress in response to a very brief, minimal physical stressor (i.e., the candle-blowing task) via a single rating before (representing anticipatory anxiety) and a single rating assessed after the task asking about peak anxiety they recalled experiencing at any point during the task. This measurement, although efficient, may have failed to capture participants’ ongoing subjective responses with sufficient granularity. With this in mind, the current study employed multiple methods of assessment to capture individuals’ subjective responses to a more intense physical stressor—the CO2-enriched air inhalation task. Most notably, participants provided continuous affective ratings during the task, beginning when they were anticipating CO2 administration and until the task was over. This continuous assessment allows for the detection of changes in participants’ affect as they occurred in real time. Participants also reported their panic symptoms and subjective anxiety at several points throughout the task. Taken together, this richer, multimodal assessment of subjective affective responses will allow for a more stringent examination of TAROT indices’ predictive utility regarding individuals’ subjective responses to a physical stressor. Given the focus on predicting responses to a physical stressor, participants completed only the physical scenarios in the TAROT task (and not the social ones).
     Data for the present study have already been collected, and ASI-3 data as well as some data corresponding to the CO2 task have been used in prior analyses. Specifically, a previous project analyzed the relationship between individuals’ anxiety sensitivity level and their subjective responses (as measured via the Subjective Units of Distress; Wolpe, 1969), panic symptoms (as measured via item 18 in the Diagnostic Symptom Questionnaire- Form B Expanded; Sanderson, Rapee, & Barlow, 1989), and skin conductance responses to the anticipatory and CO2 administration phases of the CO2  task (Espinosa, Daniel, Larrazabal, Namaky, & Teachman, 2020). Data from the TAROT task have not yet been analyzed at all.  

II. Study Aims    
1.	Further validate the TAROT task as a measure of anxiety-linked cognitive biases. This will be done by conceptually replicating analyses from Fua and Teachman (2017) regarding the psychometric properties of the TAROT task as well as the associations between TAROT indices and individuals’ anxiety sensitivity levels. 
2.	Investigate whether cognitive biases (as measured by the TAROT task) predict individuals’ subjective responses throughout the anticipatory anxiety, acute stress, and recovery phases of an in-lab physical stressor.  

III. Materials 

Tracking Affect Ratings Over Time (TAROT) task (Fua & Teachman 2017): 
	The TAROT task will be used as a measure of cognitive biases. The task was administered following procedures in Fua and Teachman (2017), with the exception that participants in this study were only presented with 18 scenarios read aloud that dealt with common physical concerns (e.g., a visit to the doctor). Each of the 18 scenarios lasted approximately 1 minute and began with an orienting statement (e.g., you go to the doctor’s office). After the orienting statement, participants were presented with an equal number of neutral, positive, and negative events (i.e., 3 of each valence); events of each valence were presented as a single set of 3 sentences related to the scenario (e.g., for the neutral event, participants heard 3 neutral occurrences relevant to going to the doctor) (see Table 1 in Fua & Teachman, 2017 for a sample scenario).  Within each scenario, valenced event sets were presented in one of six possible orders (e.g., neutral-positive-negative, negative-positive-neutral); the six valence order conditions were NP0, N0P, PN0, P0N, 0PN, and 0NP, where N = negative events, P = positive events, 0 = neutral events (e.g., for 0NP, participants heard 3 neutral events, 3 negative events, and 3 positive events, in that order). 
	Participants were asked to imagine they were experiencing each of the events in as much detail as possible. They were also asked to continuously indicate how they were feeling about the situation as they listened to the unfolding scenario. Specifically, participants were asked to indicate how positive vs. negative they felt about the information they heard using an onscreen slider bar with 5 equally-spaced tick marks labeled (from left to right) very negative, negative, neither positive nor negative, positive, and very positive. The slider bar changed in color from red (very negative), to yellow (neutral), then green (very positive). This slider yielded ratings ranging from -1,000 (very negative) to +1,000 (very positive), thus allowing the detection of fine-grained changes in participants’ affective responses.  Following each scenario, participants were asked to provide a final, overall rating for the full scenario using the same slider bar. After providing this overall affective rating, participants were instructed to return the slider to its neutral position to begin rating the next scenario (participants were not allowed to rate the next scenario until they returned the slider to the neutral position). 

Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3 (ASI-3; Taylor et al., 2007) 
	The ASI-3 is an 18-item self-report questionnaire that assesses individuals’ fear of anxiety-related symptoms (e.g., “When my stomach is upset, I worry that I might be seriously ill”). Respondents indicate how much they agree with each item using a 5-point Likert-type scale (0 = Very Little; 5 = Very Much). The ASI-3 has three domain-specific subscales—physical concerns, cognitive concerns, and social concerns. Undergraduate students completed the ASI-3 prior to enrolling in the present study and a subset were invited to participate on the basis of their responses to the physical concerns subscale. Specifically, those who scored above or below .5 standard deviations (SD) from the mean for non-clinical college students (M = 4.2, SD = 4.2; Taylor et al., 2007) were invited to participate in the study. As such, for the present study, individuals in the low anxiety sensitivity group are those who scored at or below a cutoff of 2.1, and those in the high anxiety sensitivity group scored at or above a cutoff of 6.3 on the ASI-3 physical concerns subscale. 

CO2 task
	The CO2 task was included as a stressor in this study given that it is a well-validated physical challenge for studying anxiety and panic symptoms (for a review, see Zvolensky & Eifert, 2001). Before beginning the task, research assistants told participants they would breathe room air for 14 minutes and CO2-enriched air for 4 minutes during the task. Further, they were told to anticipate the CO2-enriched air and informed about its potential effects (i.e., rapid heartbeat, dizziness, chest pressure, anxiety). Participants were not, at any point, told whether they were breathing room vs. CO2-enriched air. 
Once the task had been introduced, participants were asked to stare at a blank computer screen for 2 minutes to get a baseline physiological reading and baseline measure of panic symptoms (see DSQ-B below). Afterward, research assistants set participants up with a face mask that was connected to a bag of 7.5% CO2-enriched air. After participants were set up with the mask and given instructions, the task proceeded in three phases. 
(1) Anticipatory phase (4 minutes): during this phase, participants breathed regular room air (with regular CO2 levels) for four minutes. As mentioned above, participants were not told when they would begin breathing CO2-enriched air, and were instructed to anticipate it. Based on this, we consider this analogous to the experience of anticipating a stressor that will begin at an unspecified point in the future.  
(2) Acute stress phase (CO2 administration; 4 minutes): during this phase, participants breathed CO2-enriched air for four minutes.
(3) Recovery (10 minutes): during this phase, the CO2-enriched air was turned off and participants breathed room air for 10 minutes. 

Subjective responding during the CO2 task. 
Participants’ subjective affective responses were measured throughout the CO2 task using three measures: 
     (1) TAROT affect slider (primary subjective responding measure). Participants were asked to continuously rate how positive vs. negative they felt during the CO2 task using the same affect slider bar that was presented during the TAROT task. The affect slider was presented to participants shortly after explaining the task and setting them up with the mask. Participants were instructed to continuously self-report how positive vs. negative they felt throughout the whole task. The affect slider will serve as the primary measure of subjective responding to the CO2 task. 
  
   (2) Diagnostic Symptom Questionnaire— Form B Expanded (DSQ-B; Sanderson et al., 
1989). The DSQ-B is a 30-item self-report measure of panic symptoms. Twenty-five items ask respondents to indicate whether they experienced several specific feelings, thoughts and physical sensations associated with panic (e.g., pounding or racing heart, fear of losing control) using a dichotomous scale (yes vs. no). Two items ask respondents to rate their perceived control over their physical feelings and the avoidance of a panic attack, respectively, on a 9-point scale (0 = no control at all; 8 = total control). One item asks respondents to rate the overall sensation of panic/fear on a 9-point scale (0 = not at all noticed; 8 = very strongly felt). These items were administered as part of the larger study but are not used for these planned analyses. We will use the two items that ask respondents to rate the overall intensity of their current physical and cognitive panic symptoms, respectively, on a 9-point scale (0 = not at all noticed; 8 = very strongly felt). The intensity of physical and cognitive symptoms of panic will be used as the measure of panic symptom intensity in the present study. Panic/fear intensity will serve as a secondary measure of subjective responding to the CO2 task.   
Participants completed the DSQ-B at four discrete timepoints during the task: (1) before beginning the task, prior to putting on the CO2 mask, participants rated their in-the-moment feelings as a baseline measure; (2) participants rated their in-the-moment feelings at the beginning of the anticipatory phase, after putting on the mask; (3) after the end of the recovery phase of the CO2 task, when the mask was removed, participants were asked to think about their peak anxiety during the task and to rate their thoughts and feelings when they were experiencing that peak anxiety to reflect responding during the acute stressor; and (4) participants rated their in-the-moment feelings after the end of the recovery phase of the CO2 task, when the mask was removed, to reflect recovery. This provided measures of: (1) baseline, (2) anticipatory, (3) acute stress peak, and (4) recovery panic symptoms, respectively. 

     (3) Subjective Units of Distress (SUDS; Wolpe, 1969). The SUDS is a 1-item self-report measure of fear. Respondents orally indicate their fear level on a 100-point scale ranging from 0 (no fear) to 100 (extreme fear). Participants in this study were asked to report their SUDS at the same timepoints as the DSQ-B (except that baseline SUDS was obtained at the start of the study vs. at the start of the CO2 task). SUDS will serve as a secondary measure of subjective responding to the CO2 task.

IV. Data Preparation
Anxiety Sensitivity Index-3 – Physical Concerns subscale (ASI-3; Taylor et al., 2007) 
	Participants’ scores on the physical concerns subscale of the ASI-3 were calculated according to the measure development paper (Taylor et al., 2007). As mentioned previously, participants in this study were recruited if they scored at or below a cutoff of 2.1 or at or above a cutoff of 6.3 on the physical concerns subscale. Based on this, participants in this study were assigned to either a low anxiety sensitivity group (N = 59) or a high anxiety sensitivity group (N = 64) (final sample size for each group may change based on missing data on the TAROT and CO2 tasks). For all analyses, ASI-3 physical level will be entered as a dichotomous variable, such that individuals in the high anxiety sensitivity group will be coded as ‘1’ and those in the low anxiety sensitivity group will be coded as ‘0’.  

TAROT task 
	Following procedures in Fua and Teachman (2017), individuals’ continuous affect ratings will be used to derive 21 variables. Specifically, participants’ ratings will be used to derive the variables described below (organized by scenario section). Of note, each of the variables will be computed for each of 18 scenarios individually and analyzed within a mixed-effects (i.e., multilevel modeling) framework. 
Whole scenarios. 
1.	Mean rating. This will be calculated by taking the mean of all ratings across the scenario. 
2.	Summary rating. This will be the final rating participants provided at the end of each scenario. 
3.	Time in the negative region. This will be calculated as the percentage of time a participant spent in the negative region of the response scale throughout a given scenario.
Responses during valenced events 
4.	Inflection point response time (RT) during positive events. This will be calculated as the time it took each participant to change the direction of their response when presented with a positive event after either a neutral or negative event. If a positive event was presented as the first valenced event in a given scenario, the inflection point RT will be calculated as the time it took the participant to initiate a response from the (neutral) starting rating (same logic will apply for variables 5 and 6 below). Following procedures in Fua and Teachman (2017), changes in participants’ responses will not be counted as inflection points if they remain on the same spot in the rating scale or continue responding at the same rate as before the valenced event was introduced (this will also apply for variables 5 and 6 below). 
5.	Inflection point RT during neutral events. Analogous to #4, but following positive or negative events. 
6.	Inflection point RT during negative events. Analogous to #4, but following positive or neutral events. 
7.	Minimum rating during positive events. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided between the start and end of the positive event set. 
8.	Minimum rating during neutral events. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided between the start and end of the neutral event set.
9.	Minimum rating during negative events. This will be the (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided between the start and end of the negative event set.
10.	Maximum rating during positive events. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided between the start and end of the positive event set.
11.	Maximum rating during neutral events. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided between the start and end of the neutral event set.
12.	Maximum rating during negative events. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided between the start and end of the negative event set.
Responses after valenced events
13.	Inflection point RT following the end of positive events. This will be calculated as the time that it took each participant to change the direction of their response when presented with a new negative or neutral valence following the end of a positive event set. 
14.	Inflection point RT following the end of neutral events. This will be calculated as the time that it took each participant to change the direction of their response when presented with a new positive or negative valence following the end of a neutral event set. 
15.	Inflection point RT following the end of negative events. This will be calculated as the time that it took each participant to change the direction of their response when presented with a new positive or neutral valence following the end of a negative event set. 
16.	Minimum rating following the end of positive events. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided when presented with a new valence following the end of a positive event set. As such, this is an index of whether the prior positive events altered future responding.  
17.	Minimum rating following the end of neutral events. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided when presented with a new valence following the end of a neutral event set. As such, this is an index of whether the prior neutral events altered future responding.  
18.	Minimum rating following the end of negative events. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided when presented with a new valence following the end of a negative event set. As such, this is an index of whether the prior negative events altered future responding.  
19.	Maximum rating following the end of positive events. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided when presented with a new valence following the end of a positive event set. As such, this is an index of whether the prior positive events altered future responding.  
20.	Maximum rating following the end of neutral events. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided when presented with a new valence following the end of a neutral event set. As such, this is an index of whether the prior neutral events altered future responding.  
21.	Maximum rating following the end of negative events. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided when presented with a new valence following the end of a negative event set. As such, this is an index of whether the prior negative events altered future responding.  

Subjective responding during the CO2 task. 
Subjective responding was assessed via three measures: 
(1)	Continuous affect slider (primary measure of subjective responding). Participants’ continuous affect slider ratings will be used to derive the following 12 variables (organized by phase of the task): 
      Ratings during the anticipatory phase:
1. Inflection point RT. This will be calculated as the time that it took each participant to change the direction of their response from the neutral starting point when the affect slider was first presented (i.e., at the beginning of the anticipatory phase). (When the slider was first presented, the slider toggle was placed in the middle/at a neutral starting point). 
2.	Minimum rating. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided during the anticipatory phase.
3.	Maximum rating. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided during the anticipatory phase.
4.	Mean rating. This will be the average rating each participant provided during the anticipatory phase. 

      Ratings during the acute stress (CO2 administration) phase:
5.	Inflection point RT. This will be calculated as the time that it took each participant to change the direction of their response when the anticipatory phase ended and the acute stress phase (i.e., CO2 enriched air) began. 
6.	Minimum rating. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided during the acute stress phase.
7.	Maximum rating. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided during the acute stress phase. 
8.	Mean rating. This will be the average rating each participant provided during the acute stress phase. 
      
      Ratings during the recovery phase: 
9.	Inflection point RT. This will be calculated as the time that it took each participant to change the direction of their response when the acute stress phase ended and the recovery phase (return to regular air) began. 
10.	Minimum rating. This will be the lowest (i.e., most negative) rating each participant provided during the recovery phase.
11.	Maximum rating. This will be the highest (i.e., most positive) rating each participant provided during the recovery phase.
12.	Mean rating. This will be the average rating each participant provided during the recovery phase. 

(2)	Panic symptom intensity (secondary measure of subjective responding). We will derive the following indices of panic symptom intensity:
        2.1	Physical panic symptom intensity. This will be derived from participants’ responses to item 16 on the DSQ-B. Each participant will have one score for physical panic symptom intensity per each phase of the task. Additionally, we will compute a difference score in order to capture change in panic symptom intensity from the acute stress phase to the recovery phase of the CO2 task (i.e., we will subtract the recovery phase DSQ score from the acute stress phase DSQ score). 
        2.2	Cognitive panic symptom intensity. This will be derived from participants’ responses to item 17 on the DSQ-B. (Analogous measures to 2.1) 
Taken together, each participant will have a total of 10 DSQ scores: two corresponding to each phase of the CO2 task (i.e., baseline, anticipatory, acute stress, and recovery), and two indexing the change in their negative affect from the acute stress phase to the recovery phase of the task. 

(3)	Subjective fear (secondary measure of subjective responding). Participants orally reported their SUDS to a research assistant three times throughout the task (for more detail, see Materials section). SUDS scores range from 0 to 100. Participants’ raw SUDS scores will be used for all analyses involving subjective fear. We will also compute a difference score in order to capture change in fear from the acute stress phase to the recovery phase of the CO2 task (i.e., we will subtract the recovery phase SUDS from the acute stress phase SUDS). As such, each participant will have a total of 5 SUDS scores: one for the baseline, anticipatory, acute stress, and recovery phases, respectively, and one capturing the change in SUDS between the acute stress and recovery phases of the CO2 task. 

V. Hypotheses
*We expect the following results from Fua and Teachman (2017) will replicate:
H1. High (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will have more negative mean ratings, more negative overall summary evaluations, and spend more time in the negative (vs. positive) region of the scale during whole scenarios.  

H2. Hypotheses about responses to negative information: 
     H2a. For responses during negative events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will 
     have shorter inflection point RTs when exposed to negative events, and reach more negative 
     minimum ratings.

     H2b. For responses after negative events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will have 
     more negative minimums and less positive maximums after negative events. 

H3. Hypotheses about responses to positive information: 
     H3a. For responses during positive events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will 
     reach more negative minimums during positive events when they occur after negative 
     events (vs. after neutral events or occur as the first valence). 

     H3b. For responses after positive events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will reach 
     more negative minimum ratings after positive events. 

H4. Hypotheses about responses to neutral information: 
     H4a. For responses during neutral events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will 
     reach more negative minimums and less positive maximums during neutral events. 

     H4b. For responses after neutral events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will reach 
     more negative minimums after neutral events. 

*We found some results from Fua and Teachman (2017) surprising, and expect the following results in the present study (which would not be replicating Fua & Teachman):  
H2. Hypotheses about responses to negative information: 
     H2c. For responses after negative events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will have 
     more difficulty disengaging from negative information (i.e., longer inflection point RTs)

H3. Hypotheses about responses to positive information:
     H3c. For responses during positive events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will 
     reach less positive maximums during positive events when they occur after negative events 
     (vs. neutral events or no information). Additionally, high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals 
     will have longer inflection point RTs when exposed to positive events and reach less positive 
     maximums during these events. 

     H3d. For responses after positive events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will have 
     shorter inflection point RTs and reach less positive maximums after positive events.

H4. Hypotheses about responses to neutral information:
     H4c. For responses after neutral events: high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals will reach 
     less positive maximums after neutral events.

*We developed the following hypotheses for the present study tied to the novel acute stressor used:
Hypotheses 5-8 rationale and overview: Prior work suggests that anxiety-linked cognitive biases predict more intense/negative responses to in-lab stressors (Cabeleira et al., 2014; Gordon & Teachman, 2008). Additionally, there is evidence that individuals who are higher (vs. lower) on anxiety sensitivity experience stronger negative subjective reactions to the CO2 task (Gregor & Zvolenzky, 2008; Schmidt, & Zvolensky, 2007). Based on this prior evidence, we hypothesize that overall, more negative/less positive affect slider ratings on the TAROT task, as well as high (vs. low) anxiety sensitivity, will predict more intense/negative reactions throughout the CO2 task (i.e., we expect main effects of TAROT indicators and anxiety sensitivity on subjective responding throughout the CO2 task). In addition, we predict that the effects of TAROT indicators on individuals’ subjective responses to the CO2 task will be strongest among individuals high (vs. low) in anxiety sensitivity (i.e., an interaction effect involving TAROT indicators and anxiety sensitivity level). Below, we outline hypotheses for specific associations among TAROT indices and individuals’ responses to the CO2 task. We additionally specify instances in which we expect stronger associations between TAROT indices and subjective responses during the CO2 task due to conceptual overlap among the TAROT and CO2 task indicators (e.g., negative events during the TAROT task can be considered analogous to the acute stress phase of the CO2 task). Importantly, for all hypotheses, affect slider ratings on the CO2 task will serve as the primary measure of subjective responding during the task, while SUDS and DSQ responses will serve as secondary measures. 

H5. Individuals’ tendency to respond negatively when anticipating future negative events will predict faster and more intense/negative responses during the anticipatory phase of the CO2 task. In order to test this hypothesis, we will utilize participants’ responses to TAROT scenarios in which negative events occurred after neutral/positive event sets. Moreover, to maximize the chances that participants will have learned to expect that a negative event is forthcoming after a neutral/positive event set, we will focus on data from scenarios 5-18 (in other words, we will exclude data from the first four scenarios). Starting with scenario 5, scenarios in which negative events occurred after neutral/positive ones are conceptually analogous to the anticipatory phase of the CO2 task, given participants know a negative event is forthcoming but do not know exactly when it will begin. Therefore, we chose to focus on this subset of data to capture the cognitive bias that is likely especially predictive of individuals’ subjective responses when they are anticipating the acute stress phase of the CO2 task. Using that subset of data from the TAROT task, we expect that: 
     H5a. Shorter inflection point RTs during negative events on the TAROT will predict a shorter 
     inflection point RT when the anticipatory phase of the CO2 task begins. Additionally, this 
     association will be stronger among high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals. Of note, we 
     recognize that the strength of this association may be impacted by noise tied to how we are 
     measuring anticipatory anxiety in the CO2 task: because the inflection point RT captures 
     participants’ first movement in the CO2 task, this index may capture their processing speed 
     in addition to how quickly they experience anticipatory anxiety. Nonetheless, we consider it 
     is valuable to examine how cognitive biases predict the speed of onset of anticipatory 
     anxiety during an in-lab stressor, as not much is yet known about this association. 

     H5b. More negative ratings during neutral or positive events on the TAROT will predict more 
     negative minimum affect slider ratings, more negative mean affect slider ratings, higher 
     SUDS, and higher DSQ scores during the anticipatory phase of the CO2 task. Additionally, 
     these relationships will be stronger among high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals. 

     H5c. Less positive ratings during neutral or positive events on the TAROT will predict less 
     positive maximum affect slider ratings, more negative mean affect slider ratings, higher 
     SUDS, and higher DSQ scores during the anticipatory phase of the CO2 task. Additionally, 
     this relationship will be stronger among more (vs. less) anxiety sensitive individuals.

H6. Individuals’ tendencies to orient their attention quickly to negative information and react strongly to negative emotional stimuli will predict faster and more intense/negative responses to the acute stress phase of the CO2 task. Specifically, we expect that: 
     H6a. Shorter inflection point RTs during negative events on the TAROT will predict a shorter 
     inflection point RT when the anticipatory phase ends and the acute stress phase begins. We 
     expect this association to be particularly strong given the conceptual overlap among the 
     tasks (i.e., in both tasks, we are measuring affective responses to the onset of negative 
     stimuli). Also, we expect that this association will be stronger among high (vs. low) anxiety 
     sensitive individuals. 

     H6b. More negative minimums during negative events on the TAROT task will predict more 
     negative minimums on the affect slider, more negative mean affect slider ratings, higher 
     SUDS, and higher DSQ scores during the acute stress phase of the CO2 task. We expect this 
     association to be particularly strong given the conceptual overlap among the tasks (i.e., in 
     both tasks, we are measuring subjective responses to negative stimuli). Additionally, these 
     relationships will be stronger among high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals.

     H6c. Less positive maximums during negative events on the TAROT task will predict less 
     positive maximums on the affect slider, more negative mean affect slider ratings, higher. 
    SUDS, and higher DSQ scores during the acute stress phase of the CO2 task. We expect this 
     association to be particularly strong given the conceptual overlap among the tasks (i.e., in. 
    both tasks, we are measuring subjective responses to negative stimuli). Additionally, this. 
    relationship will be stronger among high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals.

H7. Individuals’ tendency to get “stuck” on negative information will predict more negative responses during the recovery phase of the CO2 task. Specifically, we expect that: 
     H7a. Longer inflection point RTs after negative events on the TAROT task will predict a longer 
     inflection point RT when the acute stress phase ends and the CO2 recovery phase begins. 
     We expect this association to be particularly strong given the conceptual overlap among the 
     tasks (i.e., in both tasks, we are measuring individuals’ subjective responding following the 
     end of negative stimuli). Additionally, this association will be stronger among high (vs. low) 
     anxiety sensitive individuals.

     H7b. More negative minimums after negative events on the TAROT task will predict a more 
     negative minimum affect slider rating and a more negative mean affect slider rating during 
     the CO2 recovery phase, as well as less decline in negative affect from the acute stress to 
     recovery phase for SUDS and DSQ scores. We expect these associations to be particularly 
     strong given the conceptual overlap among the tasks (i.e., in both tasks, we are measuring 
     individuals’ ability to “recover” following the end of negative stimuli). These associations will 
     be stronger among high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals. 

     H7c. Less positive maximum ratings after negative events on the TAROT task will predict a 
     less positive maximum affect slider rating and a more negative mean affect slider rating 
     during the CO2 recovery phase, as well as less decline in negative affect from the acute 
     stress to recovery phase for SUDS and DSQ scores. We expect these associations to be 
     particularly strong given the conceptual overlap among the tasks (i.e., in both tasks, we are 
     individuals’ subjective responding following the end of negative stimuli). Additionally, these 
     associations will be stronger among high (vs. low) anxiety sensitive individuals.

VI. Analytic Plan
*Replication Analyses (Hypotheses 1-4):
We will use multi-level (i.e., mixed-effects) models to test whether individuals’ level of anxiety sensitivity predicts variability in responding to valenced events in the TAROT task. We selected these models to account for the nested structure of the data, given each participant provided affective ratings to 18 different scenarios, and as such, scenarios (level-1) are nested within participants (level-2). 
We will use the lme4 package in R to conduct all analyses. We will predict each of the 21 TAROT variables (level-1 outcome variables) from a set of level-1 and level-2 predictors: scenario valence order (a six-level within-subject factor: NP0, N0P, PN0, P0N, 0PN, 0NP, modeled at level-1), anxiety sensitivity level (a dichotomous level-2 predictor), the interaction between scenario valence order and anxiety sensitivity level (cross-level interaction), and subject (entered as a random intercept to account for differences in mean responses of each participant). Separate multilevel models will be run for each of the 21 TAROT task outcome variables. As part of these models, the main effect of each predictor variable will be tested, as will the interaction effect between anxiety sensitivity and valence order (note, though, that the main effect of anxiety sensitivity is most relevant to study hypotheses). 
Given that 21 separate models will be tested, a binomial significance test will be conducted to check that the number of statistically significant main effects is not likely due to chance. This test will consider all 21 models (with 2 main predictors each) and assume a 5% chance of Type I error for each main effect. Results from this binomial test will indicate the probability of observing the (hypothesized) number of observed main effects under an expected 5% chance occurrence.  

*New Analyses (Hypotheses 5-8) 
Separate mixed-effects models will be used to predict individuals’ subjective responses during the CO2 task. In models testing hypotheses 5-7 (i.e., hypotheses about subjective responses during a given phase of the CO2 task), subjective responding variables will be predicted from anxiety sensitivity level, the relevant TAROT index, and subject (entered as a random intercept to account for individual variability in mean outcome responses).  Separate models will be run for each subjective responding outcome variable (i.e., SUDS, DSQ, and affect slider ratings). For instance, one of the models testing hypothesis 6b will predict individuals’ mean affect slider rating during the acute stress phase of the CO2 task from their anxiety sensitivity level, TAROT minimum rating during negative events, and subject. Separate models with the same predictors will be run for minimum affect slider ratings, SUDS, and DSQ scores during the acute stress phase of the CO2 task. 
As part of all models, the main effect of each predictor variable will be tested, as will the interaction effect between anxiety sensitivity and TAROT indicator. 
In order to simplify the models and reduce the number of parameters to be estimated, for analyses testing hypotheses 5-7, we will average TAROT index values across all scenarios. For instance, to arrive at a single score per participant for the variable ‘minimum rating during neutral events’, we will calculate the average of the minimum ratings during neutral events across all 18 scenarios. That is, we will derive one score per participant for each TAROT index relevant to hypotheses 5-7 and model this variable at level-2 (vs. level-1) in analyses. This procedure is similar to that utilized in Fua and Teachman (2017).

title_r: Conceptual replication and extension of health behavior theories' predictions in the context of COVID-19: Evidence across countries and over time
abstract_r: Virus mitigation behavior has been and still is a powerful means to fight the COVID-19 pandemic irrespective of the availability of pharmaceutical means (e.g., vaccines). We drew on health behavior theories to predict health-protective (coping-specific) responses and hope (coping non-specific response) from health-related cognitions (vulnerability, severity, self-assessed knowledge, efficacy). In an extension of this model, we proposed orientation to internal (problem-focused coping) and external (country capability) coping resources as antecedents of health protection and hope; health-related cognitions were assumed as mediators of this link. We tested these predictions in a large multi-national multi-wave study with a cross-sectional panel at T1 (Baseline, March-April 2020; N = 57,631 in 113 countries) and a panel subsample at two later time points, T2 (November 2020; N = 3097) and T3 (April 2021; N = 2628). Multilevel models showed that health-related cognitions predicted health-protective responses and hope. Problem-focused coping was mainly linked to health-protective behaviors (T1-T3), whereas country capability was mainly linked to hope (T1-T3). These relationships were partially mediated by health-related cognitions. We conceptually replicated predictions of health behavior theories within a real health threat, further suggesting how different coping resources are associated with qualitatively distinct outcomes. Both patterns were consistent across countries and time.

title_r: Failure to replicate associations between Toxoplasma gondii or hepatitis C virus infection and personality traits
abstract_r: Abstract Background Infections with Toxoplasma gondii (Toxo), a protozoan that can infect the brain, have been reported to alter behavior in rodents and humans; several investigators have related Toxo infection to personality traits such as novelty seeking in humans. We investigated human personality traits in relation to Toxo in Egypt, where such infection is common. Results In a community-based sample of Egyptian adults ( N = 255), Toxo infection were indexed by levels of IgG antibodies. Viruses like hepatitis C virus (HCV) have also been associated with cognitive dysfunction and mood disorders; therefore, HCV antibody titers were also assayed for comparison. The antibody levels were analyzed in relation to the Arabic version of the NEO personality inventory (NEO-FFI-3), accounting for demographic variables. No significant correlations were noted with Toxo or HCV antibody levels, after co-varying for demographic and socio-economic factors and following corrections for multiple comparisons. Conclusions Infection with Toxo or HCV infection was not associated with variations in personality traits in a sample of Egyptian adults. The possible reasons for the discordance with prior reported associations are discussed.

title_r: Resting state cortico-limbic functional connectivity and dispositional use of emotion regulation strategies: A replication and extension study
abstract_r: Neuroimaging functional connectivity analyses have shown that the negative coupling between amygdala and cortical regions is linked to better emotion regulation (ER) in experimental task settings. However, less is known about the neural correlates of ER traits or dispositions. The present study aimed to (1) replicate the findings of differential cortico-limbic coupling during resting state depending on the dispositional use of ER strategies. Furthermore, the study aimed to (2) extend prior findings by examining whether differences in cortico-limbic coupling during resting state predict behavioral and neuronal emotion regulation success in a standard emotion regulation task. To this end, N=107 healthy adults completed the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ), underwent an 8-min resting-state fMRI acquisition and completed a reappraisal task during fMRI. Functional connectivity maps of basolateral and centromedial amygdala nuclei were estimated with a seed-based approach regarding associations with regions of the prefrontal cortex, and were then correlated with ERQ scores as well as behavioral and neuronal ER success. All hypotheses and the analysis plan are preregistered at https://osf.io/8wsgu. Opposed to prior findings, we were not able to replicate a correlation of habitual ER strategy use with functional connectivity between amygdala and PFC regions. Furthermore, there was no association of behavioral and neuronal reappraisal success with functional connectivity between amygdala and insula as well as PFC. The present preregistered study calls into question the reported association between individual differences in resting state cortico-limbic connectivity and habitual use of ER strategies. However, ongoing advances in functional brain imaging and distributed network approaches may leverage the identification of reliable functional connectivity patterns that underlie successful emotion regulation.

title_r: Repairing vulnerabilities without invisible hands. A differentiated replication study on LLMs
abstract_r: Background: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) is a fast-growing branch of program repair. Recent studies show that large language models (LLMs) outperform traditional techniques, extending their success beyond code generation and fault detection. Hypothesis: These gains may be driven by hidden factors -- "invisible hands" such as training-data leakage or perfect fault localization -- that let an LLM reproduce human-authored fixes for the same code. Objective: We replicate prior AVR studies under controlled conditions by deliberately adding errors to the reported vulnerability location in the prompt. If LLMs merely regurgitate memorized fixes, both small and large localization errors should yield the same number of correct patches, because any offset should divert the model from the original fix. Method: Our pipeline repairs vulnerabilities from the Vul4J and VJTrans benchmarks after shifting the fault location by n lines from the ground truth. A first LLM generates a patch, a second LLM reviews it, and we validate the result with regression and proof-of-vulnerability tests. Finally, we manually audit a sample of patches and estimate the error rate with the Agresti-Coull-Wilson method.

title_r: OPEN ACCESS Deficits in Facial Emotion Recognition in Schizophrenia: A Replication Study with Korean Subjects
abstract_r: ObjectiveaaWe investigated the deficit in the recognition of facial emotions in a sample of medicated, stable Korean patients with schizophrenia using Korean facial emotion pictures and examined whether the possible impairments would corroborate previous findings. MethodsaaFifty-five patients with schizophrenia and 62 healthy control subjects completed the Facial Affect Identification Test with a new set of 44 colored photographs of Korean faces including the six universal emotions as well as neutral faces. ResultsaaKorean patients with schizophrenia showed impairments in the recognition of sad, fearful, and angry faces [F(1,114)=6.26, p=0.014; F(1,114)=6.18, p=0.014; F(1,114)=9.28, p=0.003, respectively], but their accuracy was no different from that of controls in the recognition of happy emotions. Higher total and three subscale scores of the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) correlated with worse performance on both angry and neutral faces. Correct responses on happy stimuli were negatively correlated with negative symptom scores of the PANSS. Patients with schizophrenia also exhibited different patterns of misidentification relative to normal controls. ConclusionaaThese findings were consistent with previous studies carried out with different ethnic groups, suggesting cross-cultural similarities in facial recognition impairment in schizophrenia. title_r: Scaling Reproducibility: An AI-Assisted Workflow for Large-Scale Replication and Reanalysis
abstract_r: Computational reproducibility is central to scientific credibility, yet verifying published results at scale remains costly. We develop an AI-assisted workflow for automated full-paper replication -- retrieving materials, reconstructing environments, executing code, and matching outputs to point estimates reported in regression tables. We define a universe of all empirical and quantitative papers from the three top political science journals (2010--2025) and measure stated data availability using automated extraction. For a stratified sample of 384 studies, we apply the workflow to conduct full-paper replication, totaling 3,523 empirical models. We find that journal verification requirements, combined with data archiving mandates, drive reproducibility: the share of fully or largely reproducible papers rises from 20.8% before DA-RT adoption to 82.5% after, and conditional on accessible replication packages, 92.1% of papers are fully or largely reproducible (234/254). As a secondary application, we apply standardized IV diagnostics to 84 studies (597 IV specifications among 1,910 replicated models), illustrating how automated execution enables systematic reanalysis across heterogeneous empirical settings.

title_r: Temperament, personality, and psychopathology in youth: A preregistered multilevel meta-analytic review and preregistered large-scale replication and extension.
abstract_r: The current pair of highly powered, preregistered studies estimates the associations between personality/temperament and youth psychopathology and evaluates the generalizability of these associations across diverse populations and research designs. In Study 1, a multilevel meta-analysis of 147 studies (k effects = 829, N = 46,369) quantified the cross-sectional associations among subjects aged 1.5-18, between five-factor model personality traits and internalizing/externalizing psychopathology dimensions within the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessments (Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001). All traits but openness evidenced bivariate associations with both psychopathology dimensions (r = |0.18-0.42|). After adjusting for the covariance between internalizing and externalizing, each dimension showed a distinct personality profile. Internalizing was associated with neuroticism (β = .42) and negative extraversion (β = -.37). Externalizing was associated with extraversion (β = .30), negative conscientiousness (β = -.46), and negative agreeableness (β = -.50). Most variance was driven by informant effects, particularly within the externalizing dimension and when personality and psychopathology were informed by the same person (i.e., mono-informant). Study 2 was a preregistered replication and extension of Study 1 in a large, demographically diverse cohort of 9- to 10-year-olds (N = 10,414; excluding diagnoses of schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders, and substance use disorders) using cross-sectional, individual-participant, item-level data and measures of temperament corollary to Study 1 personality traits. Most of Study 1's personality associations with Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessments internalizing and externalizing dimensions were replicated for higher order temperament scales (e.g., effortful control) and for their lower order scales (e.g., activation control). Again, mono-informant effects were more pronounced than cross-informant effects. Taken together, these studies provide the first quantitative synthesis of robust cross-sectional associations between personality and psychopathology in youth, highlighting the impact of mono-informant effects. Future longitudinal research may parse out directional relations as well. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title_r: The (In)Effectiveness of Political Advertising in Canada: A Conceptual Replication
abstract_r: Abstract In an effort to conceptually replicate prior work on persuasion and campaign effects, we conducted three randomized survey experiments to evaluate the persuasive effects of political advertisements during the 2025 Canadian federal election. We tested a total of 15 campaign advertisements on 3,346 respondents. Our results are consistent with what seems to be three robust findings about the effects of campaign advertising: (1) they can change candidate evaluations and vote intentions, but (2) the effects are very small, and most importantly, (3) persuasive treatment effects seem to be mostly homogeneous. We offer new empirical evidence that strengthens previous findings on the homogeneity of persuasive treatment effects of political advertising in Canada that challenges the extent to which microtargeting improves candidates and advocacy groups’ ability to sway public opinion.
